subject: mathematics
question_text: Apply the test of rank to examine whether the system x + y + z = 3, 2x + 2y − z = 3, x + y − z = 1 is consistent, and if consistent find the complete solution.

mark_split.label: Compare with the rank of [A D]
Write the equivalent equations and find z
Introduce a parameter and state the solution set

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 5 MATRICES, Long Answer question 10(i), rank-test route. The work order carries no printed page for question 10 (question 9(vii) is printed on book p.57), so no page number is asserted here rather than guessed. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+2+1+1+1+2 split pays two marks for the echelon reduction that both ranks are read from, one mark for each rank, and two for the parameter that turns "infinitely many" into a written solution set. WHY THIS CARD EXISTS ALONGSIDE ts_ipe_m1a_mat_gauss_infinite_solutions: that card solves the SAME three equations (x + y + z = 3, 2x + 2y − z = 3, x + y − z = 1) and reaches the same solution set, but it answers a different ask — "solve by the Gauss-Jordan method", which the book sets separately as question 9(vi). This question asks the student to EXAMINE CONSISTENCY, and the examiner's expected work is the rank test: reduce [A D] to echelon form, read Rank(A), read Rank[A D], compare them with each other and with the number of unknowns, and only then produce the solution. The two cards therefore differ in what earns the marks — the Gauss-Jordan card pays for the row reduction and the parameter, this one pays for the two ranks and the comparison — so both are kept. ts_ipe_m1a_mat_sqp_rank_test is the same TECHNIQUE on a different system (x + y + z = 6, x − y + z = 2, 2x − y + 3z = 9) and at SAQ length; this is the LAQ form. Working checked: det A = 0 was confirmed by expanding along R₁ and again along C₁, and the solution x = k, y = 2 − k, z = 1 was substituted back into all three original equations, where it holds for every real k (3 = 3, 3 = 3, 1 = 1). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C prints 3 long answers at 8 marks each and the student answers any 2; Matrices is one of the units that can fill a Section-C slot. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would examine this system by the rank test — say what you reduce, which two ranks you compare, what the comparison tells you, and how the complete solution is written.

steps.label: Write the augmented matrix
steps.margin_note: First mark. The rank test needs BOTH matrices, A and [A D], so write them together in the augmented form. The rule marks where the equals sign was.
steps.memory_tip: The rank test needs BOTH A and [A D], so write them together in the augmented form.
lines: The system is AX = D, where

recall.must_convey: That the augmented matrix [A | D] is written, because the rank test needs both A and [A D].
accept: write the augmented matrix A D because the test compares the rank of A with the rank of A D
form the coefficient matrix with the constants column attached
set up A given D so both ranks can be read from one reduction
augmented matrix rasta, rendu ranks oke reduction nunchi chadavali kabatti

steps.why: Rank(A) and Rank[A D] are read from the same reduced matrix, so one reduction serves both. Writing A alone would leave half the test with nothing to read.
common_mistakes: Writing A alone, which leaves Rank[A D] with nothing to read.
Putting the constants in as a fourth row instead of a fourth column.
Starting to solve before the consistency question is answered.

steps.label: Reduce to echelon form
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Columns 1 and 2 of A are identical, so clearing column 1 clears column 2 with it. Rows 2 and 3 are then proportional and one of them cancels to a row of zeros.
steps.memory_tip: Columns 1 and 2 of A are identical, so clearing column 1 clears column 2 with it.

recall.must_convey: That row operations reduce the augmented matrix to echelon form, and that the last row becomes all zeros.
accept: row reduce the augmented matrix to echelon form and the last row becomes all zeros
apply the row operations until it is in echelon shape
clear column one and the third row cancels completely
row operations tho echelon form ki teeskuravali, last row zero avthundi
reduce it and one whole row goes to zero

steps.why: Rank is the order of the largest non-zero minor, so it can be found from A itself; row reduction is simply the quickest route, and the same operations that solve a system also expose its rank.
common_mistakes: Assuming the rank is 3 because the matrix is 3×3, without testing a minor.
Treating the row of zeros as an arithmetic error and starting again.
Applying an operation to part of a row and not to the constant.

steps.label: Read the rank of A
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Rank is the order of the largest non-zero minor. Show BOTH halves: the 3×3 determinant is 0, so the rank is below 3, and one 2×2 minor is non-zero, so it is exactly 2.
steps.memory_tip: Rank is the order of the LARGEST non-zero minor. Show both halves: 3×3 is zero, one 2×2 is not.
lines: Take rows 1, 2 and columns 1, 3 of it:
This minor of order 2 is not zero,

recall.must_convey: That Rank(A) = 2, because the 3×3 determinant of the coefficient part is zero while a 2×2 minor is not.
accept: the three by three determinant is zero but a two by two minor is not so the rank of A is two
rank A is two because the largest non zero minor is of order two
det A is zero so rank is less than three and one two by two minor is non zero so it is two
det A zero, kaani oka two by two minor zero kaadu, so rank A rendu
the order of the largest non zero minor is two

steps.why: Naming a rank means naming a size. Without the non-zero 2×2 minor the argument only proves the rank is less than 3, which is not the same as proving it is 2.
common_mistakes: Stopping at det A = 0, which only shows the rank is below 3.
Counting the columns instead of the order of the largest non-zero minor.
Counting the rows instead of finding the order of the largest non-zero minor.

steps.label: Compare the two ranks
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark, and the actual test. Equal ranks means consistent. Comparing that common rank with the number of unknowns is what separates one solution from infinitely many.
steps.memory_tip: Equal ranks means consistent. Rank below the number of unknowns means infinitely many solutions.
lines: In (1) the augmented matrix also has just two
non-zero rows, so Rank[A D] = 2 as well.
But 2 < 3, the number of unknowns, so the

recall.must_convey: That Rank[A D] is also 2, that equal ranks make the system consistent, and that 2 < 3 unknowns means the solution is not unique.
accept: the rank of the augmented matrix is also two so the ranks are equal and the system is consistent
both ranks are two which is less than three unknowns so there are infinitely many solutions
equal ranks means consistent and rank less than the number of unknowns means not unique
rendu ranks rendu, so consistent, kaani unknowns moodu kabatti unique kaadu
compare rank A with rank of A D and then with the number of unknowns

steps.why: If the two ranks differed, the extra non-zero row would read 0 = a non-zero number and no solution could exist. They are equal here, so a solution exists; and because the common rank is one short of the three unknowns, one unknown stays free.
common_mistakes: Concluding consistency without writing both ranks.
Forgetting to compare the common rank with the number of unknowns.
Calling the system inconsistent because the ranks are less than 3.

steps.label: Write the equivalent equations
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Turn the surviving rows back into equations. Row 2 fixes z outright; row 1 then ties x and y together but cannot separate them.
steps.memory_tip: Turn the surviving rows back into equations: one fixes z, the other only fixes the SUM x + y.
lines: The non-zero rows of (1) are the equations

recall.must_convey: That the two surviving rows read x + y + z = 3 and z = 1, and that substituting z = 1 leaves x + y = 2.
accept: the two rows give x plus y plus z equals three and z equals one so x plus y equals two
row two gives z equals one and substituting into row one leaves x plus y equals two
convert the remaining rows to equations and find z is one so x plus y is two
row two nunchi z equals one vasthundi, substitute cheste x plus y equals two
only the sum of x and y is fixed, not x and y separately

steps.why: z is pinned down but x and y are not — only their sum is. One equation can never separate two unknowns, and that is exactly what a rank of 2 for three unknowns means.
common_mistakes: Trying to find a number for x by guessing.
Writing x + y = 3 by forgetting to substitute z = 1.
Dropping z = 1 and leaving all three letters free.

steps.label: Introduce a parameter
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. The number of free unknowns is the number of unknowns minus the rank, which is 3 − 2 = 1. Name that one k and write everything in terms of it, and say that k can be any real number.
steps.memory_tip: Free unknowns = unknowns − rank = 3 − 2 = 1. Name it k and say k can be any real number.
lines: Let x = k, where k ∈ R. Then y = 2 − k.
Check in the three original equations:

recall.must_convey: That one unknown is free because 3 − 2 = 1, giving x = k, y = 2 − k, z = 1 with k any real number.
accept: three unknowns minus rank two leaves one free so take x equals k and y is two minus k
put a parameter k for x so the solution set is k, two minus k, one
let x be k then y equals two minus k and z equals one for all real k
x ni k anukunte y equals two minus k, z equals one, k any real number
introduce a parameter and write the complete solution in terms of it
reject: x and y can be anything

steps.why: Each value of k gives one genuine solution — k = 0 gives (0, 2, 1) and k = 2 gives (2, 0, 1), and both satisfy all three original equations. The parameter is how infinitely many answers are written on one line.
common_mistakes: Writing 'infinitely many solutions' and stopping, with no solution set given.
Forgetting to state that k is a real number.
Giving one particular solution such as (0, 2, 1) as if it were the whole answer.
